You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: GPU Tsunami: TSMC, Intel and Samsung Foundry

TEXT:
TL;DR
1. TSMC is still the default choice for AI wafer foundry. TSMC remains the default choice for AI wafer foundry, but demand has already exceeded its individual capacity. Packaging bottlenecks and system-level delivery are shifting competition from wafer share to platform capacity, giving Samsung and Intel more asymmetric but less proven opportunities.
2. Advanced packaging capacity roadmap: CoWoS/SoIC, EMIB/EMIB-T, I C. Advanced packaging capacity roadmap: CoWoS/SoIC, EMIB/EMIB-T, I Cube/SAINT and OSAT spillover, covering year by year up to 2030.
3. TSMC is still the highest-confidence exposure at the wafer foundry level in AI construction. TSMC is still the highest-confidence exposure at the wafer foundry level in AI construction, but demand has exceeded TSMC’s standalone capacity. Samsung and Intel provide more asymmetric exposures to the next set of constraints, though with less validation. Samsung’s path is achieved through one-stop AI conversion.
4. Transaction implications cannot only look at single-day market moves but also at profit realization and valuation divergences. The amount matters, but account control is more important. Companies who allocate packaging slots help decide which customer can ship in a given quarter. TSMC sells wafers plus CoWoS plus SoIC; in essence, it’s selling a platform, and platform pricing is what’s measured by the bridge in Chart 1. Our cross-calculation shows that…
5. The current numbers are still relatively small. The current numbers are still relatively small. Our cross-calculation shows that Samsung’s external packaging revenues will be several hundred million USD in 2026, rising to the low single-digit billions by 2028, and reaching low to moderate tens of billions by 2030. Capacity will rise from above 10,000 wafers per month at the low end, toward the median scale of tens of thousands. This is strategically significant.
6. Intel is not yet a validated commercial wafer foundry. Intel is not yet a validated commercial wafer foundry. External revenues are still at the hundreds of millions level, and this division is still mostly in-house and unprofitable. Investable entry points are narrower: package first, wafer later.
7. 2028 scenario output in Chart 3. The 2028 scenario output in Chart 3 shows what these tasks look like in USD terms. TSMC's range is narrow because its conversion variables have been validated. The ranges for Samsung and Intel differ by about 3x between bear and bull case, which clearly shows how much is still contingent on yield, packaging capacity, and contract conversion—not demand.
To avoid losing contact, feel free to follow the backup account, which is also updated daily.
TSMC remains the default choice for AI wafer foundry, but demand now exceeds its individual capacity. Packaging bottlenecks and system-level delivery are shifting competition from wafer market share to platform capacity, giving Samsung and Intel more asymmetric but less proven opportunities. AI demand has exposed the supply chain’s lack of expansion speed. Customers are no longer just buying wafers.
I. GPU Tsunami: TSMC, Intel, and Samsung in Wafer Foundry
How AI Chips Are Shifting Foundries from Wafer Capacity to Platform Capacity
Ben Bajarin: We continue the GPU tsunami series, which frames GPU (thanks to AI) as the spark igniting the whole industry. The first report in this series studied how power semiconductors and analog control benefit from this dynamic. Higher rack density makes power delivery a larger semiconductor issue. This report tracks the same wave upstream to wafer foundry—where the problems are different but the drivers are the same: AI demand is exposing a supply chain tier not built for this pace of expansion.
Another notable dynamic is the change in what customers are buying. Wafer supply, process leadership, and per-transistor cost still matter, but they now describe a shrinking part of the decision process. Foundries are shifting from chip-level manufacturing to system-level capacity. Customers are buying a more complete deployable AI chip pathway, where wafer supply, advanced packaging, memory integration, certification, delivery timelines, and acceptable geographies must all align.
Chiplets (disaggregated design) have made this shift from chip to system platform obvious. In numbers, they are still rare—perhaps under 1% of total semiconductor shipments, maybe 10–20% of HPC/AI processor shipments—but already account for 20–35% of semiconductor revenues, and an even higher portion of leading edge value. In the AI era, we expect more high-performance chips to be built as systems comprising dies, memory, and packaging, not as monolithic chips. This dynamic benefits Intel and Samsung.
[...]
Samsung is the integration option. Logic, HBM, packaging, and Taylor grant it a one-stop AI solution. For custom ASIC teams, automotive projects, and customers constrained by HBM access, a responsible supplier is valuable. The gap is still real: advanced node yields must improve, and external packaging capacity is still far below TSMC. Tesla and Groq help validate the direction, but they're not yet proof of volume ramp.
